items.title: Destroyer returns from 11-month-deployment
items.summary:
PEARL HARBOR, Hawaii—After a 346-day deployment that included operations in the South China Sea, 12 contested transits of the Strait of Hormuz, 43 replenishments at sea and the removal of its commander 10 months in, the guided-missile-destroyer Michael Murphy returned home Thursday, welcomed by hula dancers and a rainbow stretching over the channel.

The ship was attached to the Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group for much of its deployment, though the aircraft carrier returned to its home in San Diego on Oct. 8. But any deployment-length records it may have broken were short lived. items.title: Lawsuit says Pentagon’s future warfare panel lacks transparency and balance
items.summary:
A lawsuit filed earlier this month by three government watchdog groups argues that the Defense Department assembled its Project Meridian task force to study the future of warfare in violation of federal law.

According to the complaint , the task force fails to meet requirements under the Federal Advisory Committee Act , or FACA, which include a defined structure and purpose, transparency and public input, and balanced membership.

The lawsuit alleges that the Defense Department failed to follow several procedures required under FACA. Among them, the department did not publish a notice in the Federal Register, which would allow the public to review materials and submit comments, or consult the General Services Administration, or GSA, to determine whether the research would serve the public interest.

In a statement , Donald K. Sherman, president of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, or CREW, one of the plaintiffs, said FACA “sets clear requirements about transparency and avoiding conflicts of interest.” He argued that the Defense Department must either comply with those requirements or disband the project.

When Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced Project Meridian in September, he named Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey , both owners of defense companies, and conservative politician Newt Gingrich as its directors. Nineteen others were also appointed to participate , most of whom have financial ties to the defense industry or are political allies of the administration.

items.title: Fair winds, peacoat and desert camo: Navy makes big changes to seabag
items.summary:
At the conclusion of a months-long review, the Navy is streamlining the seabag of uniforms issued to new sailors and rolling out the much-anticipated new PT gear.

According to a Navy Administrative message published on X, the service is phasing out its iconic double-breasted wool reefer/peacoat, which has been an optional uniform item since 2018. It will no longer be authorized for wear after Oct. 1, 2027. Also on borrowed time is the Navy’s rugged acrylic V-neck sweater, which is also an optional item and will see the end of authorized use next October. The wool V-neck sweater, the message adds, will continue to be authorized both afloat and ashore.

The Navy Working Uniform Type II, the Navy’s desert digital camo working uniform, is coming to a faster phaseout. Its authorized wear will terminate at the end of November.

The final item departing the seabag is the Navy’s dinner dress white jacket, a formal summer item meant to be worn with a cummerbund. After authorized wear of the jacket terminates on Oct. 1, 2027, the dinner dress blue jacket — essentially the same item, except for color — will be standard for formal wear year-round. The dinner dress blue jacket, the message notes, is a mandatory uniform item for officers in the ranks O-5 and above, and optional for the enlisted ranks and for officers through O-4.

items.title: Navy relieves commander of destroyer USS Michael Murphy
items.summary:
The Navy quietly relieved Cmdr. Caitlin Cunningham, skipper of the guided-missile destroyer USS Michael Murphy, on Sept. 27 “due to a loss of confidence to command,” a Navy official told Task & Purpose.

The relief came nine months into the ship’s 11-month deployment to the Middle East, where the USS Michael Murphy helped enforce a naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, escort tankers, launch Tomahawk cruise missiles, and defend against Iranian drone and missile attacks. The USS Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group, which the Murphy was a part of, was later awarded the Presidential Unit Citation. 

USNI News first reported on Cunningham’s removal .

No reason was given for Cunningham’s firing. The Navy regularly uses the term “loss of confidence” as a catchall for the many reasons a commander can be relieved. The term is used for everything from mishaps onboard the vessel to personal misconduct by an officer. 

Cmdr. David Nicholas has helmed the destroyer since Cunningham was relieved.

items.title: The Air Force maverick ‘who changed the art of war’
items.summary:
During World War I, fighter pilots became “knights of the air,” — romanticized as noble, masculine heroes who guarded the ground from violence above. That mythology lasted, creating a heritage that still tinges new fighter pilots with pride.

“Military culture is different from civilian culture, military aviation culture is distinct from both, but fighter pilot culture is a world unto itself,” writes Michael W. Hankins in Flying Camelot: The F-15, the F-16, and the Weaponization of Fighter Pilot Nostalgia .

However, things were different for Vietnam War pilots. Century Series fighters had struggled in the conflict’s air combat and the Air Force’s front-line fighter was the two-seater F-4 Phantom. The mythos of the fearless, individualistic fighter and the desire for turn-and-burn dogfights seemingly evaporated. 

Col. John Richard Boyd and his “Fighter Mafia” strove to change that. 

Born in Erie, Pennsylvania, in 1927, Boyd entered the U.S. Army Air Forces at the tail end of World War II, spending 12 uneventful months in Japan before his discharge in 1947. At the outbreak of the Korean War, Boyd reenlisted and was assigned to Nellis Air Force Base in Arizona, where he trained in a North American F-86 Sabre before logging a slew of combat hours in Korea — and, in the final few weeks of the war, was credited with damaging a MiG-15.

Ordered back to Nellis, Boyd began training to become a flight instructor, and he soon earned a reputation for being unafraid of criticizing superior officers.

His detractors would later call him profane, crude — perhaps even treasonous.…
items.t: The Air Force maverick ‘who changed the art of war’

items.title: The Pentagon brings back World War II-era OSS for special operations missions, funding
items.summary:
The Office of Strategic Services, the intelligence and commando arm of the U.S. military during World War II, might live again, at least in name, as part of a reorganization of the Pentagon’s special operations civilian leadership. 

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued a memo on Nov. 2 that renames the Assistant Secretary of Defense for Special Operations and Low-Intensity Conflict to the Assistant Secretary of War for the Office of Strategic Services, though permanently doing so would require congressional approval. 

As part of the renaming, Hegseth wants to move the assistant secretary of defense for special operations and low-intensity conflict position higher up the leadership ladder, marking the latest in a decades-long effort to put civilian oversight of special operations forces (SOF) on an even footing with the secretaries of the Army, Navy, and Air Force.

items.title: US Air Force adopts new Force Design focusing on sensors and autonomy
items.summary:
The U.S. Air Force has changed its strategic outlook, announcing a new Force Design 2026 that replaces its previous standards established in 2024. 

“The U.S. Air Force Force Design 2026 provides an enduring framework for identifying operational problems, shaping capability development, and informing modernization priorities – ensuring the Air Force evolves how it fights, and that it fields a winning force,” an Air Force spokesperson told Military Times.

“The Force Design is a classified document so there is no releasable copy,” the spokesperson said. 

In October 2024, the service announced it would follow guidance set out in a “One Force Design” document, signed by then-Chief of Staff Gen. David Allvin and said to be the “North Star” for Air Force modernization plans.

It introduced three distinct mission areas, effectively divvying up air defenses against unmanned aircraft systems. The Air Force’s drone-killing capabilities were classified in the 2024 document in categories of short-range, long-range and intercontinental defense, respectively.

Although the new Force Design 2026 document is classified, the service’s release hints at some key changes.

items.title: Destroyer That Has Been Deployed Longer Than Any Since WWII Returns Home
items.summary:
Two guided-missile destroyers assigned to the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group (CSG), USS Spruance and USS Michael Murphy , have returned home after 357- and 346-day deployments, respectively, more than a month after the carrier they escorted returned to San Diego . Both are reportedly longer than any previous destroyer cruise since World War II. However, the record may not hold for long, as USS John Finn is on pace to surpass both.

Spruance pulled out of Naval Base San Diego on November 21, 2025, alongside Nimitz class aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln , on what the crews expected would be a routine deployment to the Western Pacific. Murphy linked up with the strike group 10 days later as it sailed past her homeport at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam, Hawaii.

Both ships, which endured conditions just as grueling as Lincoln , if not more so, returned to their homeports over the past 24 hours. Spruance departed Pearl Harbor on November 6, according to MarineTraffic , and arrived in San Diego today. Planet Labs satellite imagery reviewed by TWZ showed Murphy in Guam on November 3, her last stop before transiting northeast back to Pearl Harbor and pulling into port yesterday.

USS Michael Murphy returns home to Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam on November 12. U.S. Navy photo 

The extended deployments are a reminder of how the war with Iran and the blockade that followed have pushed the Navy’s surface fleet past the seven-month cruises it long treated as standard. Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle told Sailors recently to expect the new normal for deployments…

items.title: Judges close part of ICC Afghanistan investigations that could look at US troops
items.summary:
Judges at the International Criminal Court have issued a decision to formally close part of the prosecutor’s investigations into Afghanistan that previously looked at alleged crimes by U.S. troops and to focus only on actions of the Taliban since 2021, court documents show.

The decision by the chamber formally closes not only the line of inquiry into alleged crimes by U.S. troops, which had already lain dormant since 2021, but also a probe into the Islamic State Khorasan (ISIS-K) militia. The office of the prosecutor told Reuters on Friday it had appealed the decision but could not give further details.

It is the latest step in a legal tussle between prosecutors and judges about the Afghanistan case, and comes after the United States issued institutional sanctions against the court, citing U.S. opposition to arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials and ​the investigation into actions of U.S. soldiers in Afghanistan.

This year, judges ordered prosecutors to split their Afghanistan inquiries into two separate probes — one focusing on the alleged crimes committed by the Taliban since 2021, and the other on the original Afghanistan inquiry, which also looked at alleged war crimes by U.S. troops but has shifted towards looking at the ISIS-K militia.

Judges said they had taken the decision to close part of the case because prosecutors had not shown they would be able to effectively investigate allegations in Afghanistan apart from the Taliban probe. The splitting of the cases means the arrest warrants issued against four Afghan Taliban leaders remain in effect.

items.title: Congress has access to IVF. Military families like mine do not.
items.summary:
Editor’s note: The views expressed in this op-ed are solely the author’s and do not reflect the official positions or policies of the U.S. government or the Department of Defense. 

The United States asks military families like mine to accept a lot: deployments, repeated moves, long separations and lives built around the needs of the service. It should not deny us the medical care we need to have children.

TRICARE, the health insurance program for our nation’s service members and their families, refuses to cover in vitro fertilization in most cases, denying service members the tools they need to start a family. Congress has not yet fixed this failure, but it can now.

As lawmakers consider this year’s defense bill, they have another opportunity to expand IVF coverage. They have come close before: Last year, both chambers included IVF coverage in their versions of the bill, only to drop it from the final legislation.

For my family, those decisions have real consequences. 

My wife and I want children. But every conversation we have about parenthood runs into the same hard fact: I inherited the BRCA1 mutation, which is linked to prostate and pancreatic cancer in men and substantially higher risks of breast and ovarian cancer in women. Any child we conceive would have a 50% chance of inheriting it, and with it, their own significant cancer risk.

This is an all too familiar story in my family.

items.t: Congress has access to IVF. Military families like mine do not.

items.title: US Army names officer held on ‘allegations of espionage’

An Army official identified Lt. Col. Brandon Carroll Tyner as the U.S. soldier arrested earlier this week in the United Kingdom for reportedly assisting Russian intelligence in what FBI Director Kash Patel described as “allegations of espionage.” 

Tyner, 41, began serving in the Army as a human resources officer — military occupational specialty 42H — in January 2008, the official told Military Times. Tyner’s deployments included tours in Afghanistan, Qatar and Iraq.

At the time of his arrest, he was assigned to Imjin Barracks , a British Army base near Gloucestershire, England, which hosts NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. His arrest came shortly after the U.S. removed aircraft from British military bases over an unrelated reported threat from Iran. 

Tyner was arrested under Sections 1 and 3 of Britain’s 2023 National Security Act and the Army said officials were investigating two locations in Gloucestershire. Counter Terrorism Policing London is leading the investigation and the accused officer remains in custody at a London police station.

items.title: Entire command team of USS South Dakota relieved following grounding incident
items.summary:

The firing was first reported by the Connecticut newspaper The Day , which said that Cmdr. Dan Goodwin was removed from the post on Oct. 14. Alongside Goodwin, the submarine’s executive officer and chief of the boat — the top enlisted leader aboard a submarine — were also relieved that day. Two members of Congress wrote to acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao and Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle over the matter, accusing the Navy of failing to notify the House Armed Services Committee about the command triad’s removal.

The letter , from Rep. Joe Courtney (D-Conn.), the ranking member of the House Seapower and Projection Forces Subcommittee, and Adam Smith (D-Wash.), the ranking member of the House Armed Services Committee, cites The Day’s reporting and says the committee had not been informed for nearly a month, which they called “unacceptable.”

“In the wake of the collisions affecting USS Fitzgerald (DDG 62), USS John S. items.title: The Air Force’s Newest Trainer Is An Aerobatic Plane

The U.S. Air Force unveiled its newest aircraft today by flying them over the Air Force Academy , where they will be used to train a future generation of pilots and serve as the basis for a new aerial demonstration team. items.title: Second world war ‘brain’ bunker in cliffs of Dover opens to public

It has been kept secret for decades, buried four metres deep into the white cliffs of Dover. But from Friday, members of the public will finally be able to visit a pioneering command bunker that was ordered by Winston Churchill and proved a vital defence during the second world war.

The Fan Bay plotting room, which is encased in concrete, housed the first land-based computer-aided targeting system. This acted as a “brain” for a gun battery that was used to defend Dover and attack German ships in the Channel, according to Jon Barker, who led the excavation project for the National Trust.

items.title: Keep US troops in NATO’s KFOR
items.summary:
As the Pentagon finalizes its review of U.S. force posture in Europe, one relatively small commitment deserves protection from the budget axe: the roughly 600 American troops serving in NATO’s Kosovo Force. They barely register in a debate about brigades and billion-dollar line items, but they keep a hard-won peace in the Balkans, and pulling them out would save almost nothing while handing Moscow a cheap strategic win.

KFOR was deployed in June 1999 under NATO command, after the alliance bombed Yugoslavia to stop the violence perpetrated by Slobodan Milosevic’s Serbian forces against ethnic Albanians. Kosovo declared independence in 2008, but Serbia, backed by Russia and China, still refuses to recognize it.

The Europe posture review is a legitimate exercise. After years of urging European allies to shoulder more of their own conventional defense, the Trump administration is right to ask hard questions about where American forces add unique value and where Europe can step up given suitable time to develop their capabilities and capacities. But KFOR is a mission in which the American role is not easily replaced, because it is as much political as military, and where a wrong call risks instability…
